cards.front: Which histamine receptor types are clinically relevant, and what is the role of H3 and H4?
cards.back: H1 and H2 are the main clinically targeted types. H3 is mainly a presynaptic autoreceptor in the brain that limits histamine release; KDT lists no H3 drug in use, but GG14 notes pitolisant, an H3 inverse agonist, is approved for narcolepsy. H4, cloned in 2001, is on eosinophils, mast cells and basophils and promotes their chemotaxis.

cards.front: What are the signalling pathways of H1 and H2 receptors?
cards.back: H1 is Gq-coupled: PIP2 hydrolysis gives IP3 and DAG, releasing intracellular Ca2+ and activating protein kinase C. H2 is Gs-coupled: adenylyl cyclase is stimulated and cAMP rises.

cards.front: Describe the triple response produced by intradermal histamine.
cards.back: Red spot from intense capillary dilatation; wheal from fluid leaking out of capillaries and venules; flare, a surrounding redness from arteriolar dilatation that is driven by an axon reflex.

cards.front: Why is histamine inactive when given orally?
cards.back: It is rapidly broken down by oxidation and methylation, and the liver degrades all histamine absorbed from the intestine before it reaches the circulation.

cards.front: Why are first-generation H1 antihistamines sedating, and which ones are the most sedating?
cards.back: They cross the blood-brain barrier and block central H1 receptors that help maintain wakefulness. Diphenhydramine, promethazine, hydroxyzine and dimenhydrinate are the highly sedating members, while chlorpheniramine and clemastine are only mildly sedating.

cards.front: Why were terfenadine and astemizole withdrawn, and how does fexofenadine avoid this problem?
cards.back: Both caused torsades de pointes through blockade of cardiac delayed rectifier K+ channels, especially at higher doses or with CYP3A4 inhibitors. Fexofenadine, the active metabolite of terfenadine, blocks these channels only weakly and is minimally metabolised, so it does not prolong the QTc interval.

cards.front: Why are H1 antihistamines ineffective in bronchial asthma?
cards.back: Leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4) and PAF are more important mediators of human asthma than histamine. Also, the antihistamine may not reach concentrations high enough to block the large amounts of histamine released locally in the bronchi.

cards.front: Why is adrenaline, not an antihistamine, the life-saving drug in anaphylactic shock?
cards.back: H1 antihistamines act slowly and only block histamine effects. In anaphylaxis, leukotrienes and PAF contribute substantially to the fall in blood pressure, so adrenaline is the first-line drug and antihistamines play a secondary role.

cards.front: What is betahistine, what is it used for, and what are its contraindications?
cards.back: An orally active histamine analogue with some H1 selectivity, used for vertigo in Meniere's disease, probably by improving blood flow in the inner ear. It is contraindicated in patients with asthma and peptic ulcer.

cards.front: What additional actions does cyproheptadine have beyond H1 blockade, and what are its uses?
cards.back: It also blocks 5-HT2A receptors and is sedating. Uses include pruritus, appetite stimulation (including off-label use in underweight patients), and control of carcinoid intestinal symptoms and SSRI-induced priapism.

cards.front: Short note: Classification of H1 antihistaminics

points: Most agents have a substituted ethylamine side chain

Moderately sedative: pheniramine, cyproheptadine, cinnarizine
Mildly sedative: chlorpheniramine, triprolidine, clemastine
Marketed after 1980; largely nonsedating
Higher H1 selectivity with no anticholinergic effects
Some also reduce release or action of leukotrienes, PAF and cytokines
Fexofenadine, loratadine, desloratadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine
Azelastine (nasal spray), mizolastine, ebastine, rupatadine (also PAF antagonist)

points: Stored mainly in mast cell granules, bound to acidic protein and heparin
Released by exocytosis when granules are extruded

Dominant physiological stimulus for acid secretion
Acts on H2 receptors to activate the parietal cell proton pump
Potentiates the effects of gastrin and acetylcholine
Released from mast cells after antigen cross-links IgE
Causative in urticaria, angioedema and bronchoconstriction
Not involved in delayed-type allergic reactions
Mediates itch and pain at sensory nerve endings
Wakefulness and appetite in the brain
Increases leukocyte adhesion in inflammation

points: Control itching, urticaria, seasonal hay fever and allergic conjunctivitis
Palliative only: they do not block antigen-antibody reaction
Not useful in asthma, and secondary to adrenaline in anaphylaxis
Promethazine, diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, meclozine for prophylaxis
Give about one hour before travel

Pruritus, insect bites, dermographism
Sedation and short-term hypnosis, though less dependable than benzodiazepines
Parkinsonism and drug-induced dystonia through anticholinergic action

Alcohol and other CNS depressants add to the effect
Paradoxical restlessness or insomnia in a few individuals
Dry mouth, constipation, urinary hesitancy and blurred vision
Adds to effects of atropine, phenothiazines and tricyclic antidepressants

Promethazine can cause fatal respiratory depression in children up to 2 years
Caution in pregnancy; teratogenic in animals only
Central excitation, convulsions, hypotension and belladonna-like features
Death from respiratory and cardiovascular failure

First generation: sedative and anticholinergic, graded by sedation

Block histamine-induced bronchoconstriction, smooth muscle contraction and the wheal and itch of the triple response
Block low-dose histamine hypotension; high doses need H1 plus H2 blockade
Antiallergic action without suppressing the antigen-antibody reaction
Urticaria, hay fever, allergic conjunctivitis and angioedema
Motion sickness, vertigo and nausea
Sedation, pruritus and parkinsonism
Sedation and psychomotor impairment with first-generation drugs
Anticholinergic effects and fall in BP after intravenous use
Torsades with terfenadine and astemizole
No sedation and no potentiation of alcohol or benzodiazepines
Little or no anticholinergic action
Some also inhibit release or action of leukotrienes and PAF

cards.front: Essay: Histamine in physiology and allergy

points: Tissue amine, imidazolylethylamine derived from histidine
Early work by Dale linked its actions to allergic reactions
H1 (Gq), H2 (Gs), H3 (Gi/Go, presynaptic in brain), H4 (immune cells)
Classification by selective agonists and antagonists
Arteriolar and capillary dilatation with flushing and fall in BP
Increased capillary permeability and oedema
Bronchoconstriction, mainly through H1
H2-mediated acid secretion through cAMP and the proton pump
H2 blockers such as cimetidine and famotidine reduce acid secretion (some ranitidine preparations were withdrawn because of contamination)
Released by IgE-mediated degranulation and by histamine releasers
Urticaria, angioedema and bronchospasm
Not responsible for delayed reactions
Transmitter for itch and pain
Regulates wakefulness, body temperature and growth and repair

cards.front: Classify: histamine receptors
cards.text: H1 is {{Gq}}-coupled and raises IP3 and Ca2+; H2 is {{Gs}}-coupled and raises {{cAMP}}; H3 is a {{presynaptic autoreceptor}} in the brain; H4 is found on {{eosinophils}}, mast cells and basophils.

cards.front: Classify: first-generation H1 antihistaminics by sedation
cards.text: Highly sedative: {{diphenhydramine}}, {{dimenhydrinate}}, {{promethazine}} and {{hydroxyzine}}; moderately sedative: {{pheniramine}}, {{cyproheptadine}} and {{cinnarizine}}; mildly sedative: {{chlorpheniramine}}, {{triprolidine}} and {{clemastine}}.

cards.front: Classify: second-generation H1 antihistaminics
cards.text: Second-generation (nonsedating) H1 antihistaminics: {{fexofenadine}}, {{loratadine}}, {{desloratadine}} (active metabolite of loratadine), {{cetirizine}}, {{levocetirizine}} (its active enantiomer), {{azelastine}} (nasal spray), {{mizolastine}}, {{ebastine}} and {{rupatadine}}.

cards.front: Classify: antihistamine-related drugs by use
cards.text: Motion sickness prophylaxis: {{promethazine}}; Meniere's vertigo: {{betahistine}}; first-line for anaphylaxis: {{adrenaline}}; sedative antihistamine used in drug-induced dystonia: {{promethazine}}.

cards.front: Describe the synthesis and degradation of 5-HT.
cards.back: 5-HT is made from L-tryptophan: tryptophan hydroxylase forms 5-hydroxytryptophan, which is decarboxylated to 5-HT. It is degraded mainly by MAO-A to 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid. It is taken up into platelets and nerve endings by the serotonin transporter, which SSRIs and tricyclics inhibit, and its vesicular storage (VMAT-2) is blocked by reserpine.

cards.front: How are the 5-HT receptor families classified by their signalling?
cards.back: 5-HT1 receptors (Gi/Go) reduce cAMP. 5-HT2 receptors (Gq) generate IP3 and DAG. 5-HT4, 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 (Gs) raise cAMP. 5-HT3 is not G-protein coupled but a ligand-gated cation channel that depolarises nerve endings quickly.

cards.front: Which 5-HT receptor do triptans act on, and what does it do in cranial vessels?
cards.back: 5-HT1B/1D. Stimulation constricts dilated cranial vessels, including carotid arteriovenous shunts, and reduces release of inflammatory neuropeptides from perivascular nerves. Sumatriptan is the prototype selective agonist.

cards.front: What is the role of 5-HT1A agonists such as buspirone?
cards.back: Buspirone, gepirone and ipsapirone are azapirones that act as partial agonists at 5-HT1A receptors. They are anxiolytics that do not cause sedation.

cards.front: Which receptor mediates the emetic reflex, and which antagonist is the prototype?
cards.back: 5-HT3 receptors on nerve endings in the gut wall (myenteric plexus), in the area postrema and in the nucleus tractus solitarius. Ondansetron is the prototype selective 5-HT3 antagonist, used against vomiting from highly emetic cytotoxic drugs and radiotherapy.

cards.front: What does 5-HT do to platelets?
cards.back: Acting on 5-HT2A receptors it changes platelet shape and causes weak aggregation, but it does not induce the release reaction. Platelets store and release 5-HT, which amplifies aggregation with collagen and other mediators.

cards.front: Why was methysergide withdrawn, and what was it used for?
cards.back: It is a potent 5-HT2A/2C antagonist used for migraine prophylaxis, carcinoid and postgastrectomy dumping syndrome. It was withdrawn because it caused fibrosis in the abdomen, lungs and endocardium.

cards.front: Why are ergot alkaloids poorly suited to oral migraine treatment?
cards.back: Oral bioavailability of the amino-acid ergots (ergotamine) and their hydrogenated derivatives is below 1 percent, due to slow and incomplete absorption and high first-pass metabolism. Caffeine improves absorption of ergotamine.

cards.front: Sumatriptan: doses and main contraindications.
cards.back: Oral 50 to 100 mg at the onset of an attack; may be repeated once within 24 hours, but not if the first dose failed. SC 6 mg (acts in 10 to 20 min, also repeatable once in 24 h) when oral use is impractical or pain builds quickly; nasal spray is an alternative. Contraindicated in ischaemic or vasospastic coronary disease, stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic or basilar migraine, ischaemic bowel disease and uncontrolled hypertension. Do not give within 24 hours of an ergot or another triptan, or within 2 weeks of an MAO inhibitor; combining with SSRIs or SNRIs risks serotonin syndrome.

cards.front: What is the first-line treatment for a mild migraine attack, and what adjunct is useful for nausea?
cards.back: Simple analgesics such as paracetamol (0.5 to 1 g) or aspirin (300 to 600 mg) taken at the first sign of an attack. Metoclopramide, given orally or by injection, relieves the nausea and gastric stasis that delay absorption.

cards.front: Short note: 5-HT receptor subtypes and their clinical relevance

points: Gi/Go coupled; mainly autoreceptors that inhibit 5-HT release
5-HT1A in raphe nuclei: buspirone as partial agonist
5-HT1B/1D in cranial vessels: triptans
Gq coupled; IP3 and DAG pathway
5-HT2A is the main postjunctional receptor for smooth muscle contraction and platelet activity
Ketanserin and clozapine block 5-HT2A
Ligand-gated cation channel that depolarises nerve endings quickly
Mediates pain, itch, chemoreflex and emesis
Ondansetron blocks it as an antiemetic
5-HT4 is Gs coupled and increases peristalsis and secretion
Cisapride and renzapride are 5-HT4 agonists (cisapride restricted because of QT prolongation); prucalopride is a specific 5-HT4 agonist
5-HT5, 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 are mainly central, with uncertain function

cards.front: Short note: Triptans

points: Selective 5-HT1B/1D agonists
Constrict dilated cranial vessels and reduce neurogenic inflammation
First-line for moderate to severe migraine not relieved by analgesics
Oral bioavailability about 15 percent; faster and more effective by s.c. injection or nasal spray
Metabolised by MAO-A; half-life about 2 hours
Tends to relieve the nausea and vomiting of migraine
Chest and head tightness, paraesthesias and dizziness
Serious but rare: coronary vasospasm, bradycardia and myocardial infarction
Rizatriptan is more potent with higher oral bioavailability
Naratriptan and frovatriptan have longer half-lives, so fewer recurrences
Lasmiditan: 5-HT1F agonist (not a triptan) with fewer cardiovascular effects, for patients with cardiovascular risk

cards.front: Short note: Prophylaxis of migraine

points: Two or three or more attacks per month
Attacks disabling despite treatment
Contraindication to triptans or ergots
Propranolol is first choice; starts at 40 mg twice daily, up to 160 mg twice daily
Effect seen in about 4 weeks; pindolol is not useful
Amitriptyline 25 to 50 mg at bedtime, more side effects than propranolol
Flunarizine 10 to 20 mg daily, weak calcium channel blocker
Valproate and topiramate, mainly for patients refractory to others
CGRP blockers: monoclonal antibodies erenumab (receptor), fremanezumab and galcanezumab; small-molecule receptor antagonist rimegepant

cards.front: Short note: Ergot alkaloids in migraine

points: Amine alkaloid: ergometrine
Amino acid alkaloids: ergotamine and ergotoxine
Semisynthetic: dihydroergotamine, codergocrine, bromocriptine, methysergide
Partial agonist or antagonist at adrenergic and 5-HT1/5-HT2 receptors
Most effective ergot for migraine if given early in the attack
Oral or sublingual dose 1 mg every 30 minutes, maximum 6 mg
Less vasoconstrictor and less emetic than ergotamine
Preferred for parenteral use
Largely replaced by triptans
No prophylactic value; regular use can cause a rebound headache
Contraindicated in sepsis, ischaemic heart disease and pregnancy

cards.front: Essay: Pathogenesis and drug management of migraine

points: Unilateral pulsatile headache lasting 4 to 48 hours
Nausea, vomiting, photophobia, sonophobia and, in some, aura
Two types: migraine with aura and migraine without aura
Vascular theory: initial vasoconstriction and shunting of blood
Neurogenic theory: spreading cortical depression and neurogenic inflammation
Mediators include 5-HT, substance P, neurokinin, CGRP and nitric oxide
Blood and urinary 5-HT changes during attacks
5-HT releasers can precipitate attacks
Serotonergic drugs prevent, abort or terminate attacks
Mild: simple analgesics or NSAIDs with an antiemetic
Moderate: NSAID combinations or a triptan or ergot
Severe: triptan or ergot with antiemetic, sometimes with a longer-acting NSAID
Propranolol, amitriptyline, flunarizine, valproate, topiramate; CGRP receptor antibody erenumab
Continue 6 months or more, then review whether still needed

cards.front: Essay: Serotonin receptors and the drugs that act on them

points: Serotonin (5-HT) is a neurotransmitter, vasoactive and gut-active amine
Synthesised from tryptophan and mainly stored in enterochromaffin cells and platelets
Four families with 14 subtypes, classified by molecular cloning
Signalling by Gi, Gq, Gs, or direct channel gating (5-HT3)
Direct and reflex effects on vessels, gut, bronchi and platelets
Triphasic blood pressure response in animals
Potent stimulant of intestinal peristalsis
Neurotransmission in mood, sleep, appetite and pain
Role in emesis, haemostasis, carcinoid syndrome and migraine
Agonists: LSD (nonselective), buspirone, triptans, cisapride
Antagonists: cyproheptadine, methysergide, ketanserin, ondansetron, clozapine
Triptans for acute migraine
Ondansetron for chemotherapy-induced vomiting
Atypical antipsychotics for schizophrenia through 5-HT2A blockade

cards.front: Classify: 5-HT receptor families
cards.text: 5-HT1 receptors {{decrease}} cAMP through Gi; 5-HT2 receptors act through {{Gq}}; 5-HT3 is a {{ligand-gated cation channel}}; 5-HT4, 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 {{increase}} cAMP.

cards.front: Classify: 5-HT receptor subtypes and their drugs
cards.text: Buspirone is a partial agonist at {{5-HT1A}}; sumatriptan is an agonist at {{5-HT1B/1D}}; ketanserin blocks {{5-HT2A}}; ondansetron blocks {{5-HT3}}; cisapride is an agonist at {{5-HT4}}.

cards.front: Classify: acute migraine treatment by severity
cards.text: Mild: {{paracetamol}} or NSAIDs; moderate: NSAID combinations, a {{triptan}} or an {{ergot alkaloid}}; severe: triptan or ergot plus an {{antiemetic}} such as {{metoclopramide}}.

cards.front: Classify: migraine prophylaxis agents
Name the precursor and the two main enzymatic pathways for eicosanoid synthesis.
cards.back: The precursor is arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid), released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2. The cyclooxygenase pathway makes prostaglandins, thromboxanes and prostacyclin. The lipoxygenase pathway (5-LOX) makes leukotrienes. Eicosanoids are not stored; they are made when needed.

cards.front: How do COX-1 and COX-2 differ in function?
cards.back: COX-1 is expressed constitutively in most cells and makes prostanoids for housekeeping functions: gastric mucosal protection, platelet TXA2 and renal function. COX-2 is induced by cytokines, shear stress and growth factors and is the main source of prostanoids in inflammation (pain, fever) and cancer. The split is not absolute: COX-2 also contributes constitutively in some tissues, such as gastric epithelium. Selective COX-2 inhibitors include celecoxib and etoricoxib.

cards.front: How does aspirin differ from other NSAIDs in inhibiting COX?
cards.back: Aspirin acetylates a serine residue on COX and inhibits it irreversibly. Other NSAIDs are competitive and reversible. Because platelets cannot make new COX-1 and the vessel wall can, low-dose aspirin inhibits platelet thromboxane for days.

cards.front: What are the opposing actions of platelet TXA2 and endothelial PGI2?
cards.back: TXA2, made by platelets, promotes aggregation and vasoconstriction. PGI2, made by the endothelium, inhibits aggregation and causes vasodilatation. The two act as a balanced system that keeps blood flowing and allows plugging when a vessel is injured.

cards.front: Which prostanoids constrict bronchi, and which dilate them?
cards.back: PGF2alpha, PGD2 and TXA2 constrict bronchi, more strongly than histamine. PGE2 is a powerful bronchodilator and PGI2 a mild one. Inhaled PGE2 is not clinically useful because it irritates the airway and its action is brief.

cards.front: What are the gastroprotective actions of PGE2?
cards.back: PGE2 reduces basal and stimulated acid and pepsin secretion, suppresses gastrin release, and increases mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow. The ulcer-causing effect of NSAIDs is attributed to losing this protection.

cards.front: Which leukotriene receptor antagonists are used in asthma, and what do they block?
cards.back: Montelukast and zafirlukast block the cysLT1 receptor, which is mainly on bronchial and intestinal smooth muscle and binds LTD4 more avidly than LTC4. They are useful antiasthmatic drugs.

cards.front: What is platelet activating factor chemically, and how is it made?
cards.back: It is acetylglyceryl ether phosphorylcholine, with an ether-linked alkyl chain of 16 or 18 carbons. It is made on demand from membrane phospholipids, with the second step rate-limiting. It is active at subnanomolar concentrations.

cards.front: Carboprost: what is it, and how is it used in postpartum haemorrhage?
cards.back: Carboprost is 15-methyl PGF2-alpha; the methyl group prolongs its action. For PPH from uterine atony not responding to oxytocin and ergometrine: 0.25 mg (250 mcg) IM, repeated every 30 to 120 minutes if needed (KDT); Katzung cites about 80% success. It is also used for second-trimester and missed abortion. Adverse effects: vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, flushing and transient bronchoconstriction.

cards.front: Which PGF2alpha analogues are first-line for open-angle glaucoma and how do they work?
cards.back: Latanoprost, travoprost and bimatoprost are FP receptor agonists. They lower intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral and trabecular outflow of aqueous humour, and are non-irritating compared with the parent PGF2alpha.

cards.front: Short note: Prostaglandins in obstetrics

points: First trimester: suction evacuation is the procedure of choice
Medical abortion: mifepristone 600 mg orally, then misoprostol 400 mcg orally 2 days (48 h) later; KDT gives this for up to 7 weeks (49 days), Katzung through 70 days; success above 90% up to 49 days
Misoprostol route: KDT notes many prefer vaginal (fewer side effects); Katzung recommends oral because vaginal use was linked to sepsis
Midterm abortion: PGs make the oxytocin-resistant midterm uterus responsive (extra-amniotic PGE2 then oxytocin infusion, or intra-amniotic PGF2-alpha); mifepristone pretreatment improves efficacy
Low-dose PGE2 softens an unfavourable cervix without affecting uterine motility
Dinoprostone is used to induce or augment labour
PGs are not better than oxytocin for induction at term
Carboprost 0.25 mg IM for uterine atony when ergometrine and oxytocin fail
Carboprost is also used in midterm and missed abortion
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, uterine cramps and vaginal bleeding
Fever, flushing, shivering and fall in BP

cards.front: Short note: Non-obstetric clinical uses of prostaglandin analogues

points: Latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost for glaucoma
Misoprostol (PGE1 analogue) to heal peptic ulcer, especially in patients who must continue NSAIDs
Alprostadil (PGE1) keeps the ductus arteriosus open in neonates until surgery
Pulmonary arterial hypertension: epoprostenol (PGI2) and the analogues treprostinil and iloprost; selexipag is an oral IP receptor agonist
Epoprostenol protects platelets during haemodialysis and bypass
PGI2 or PGE1 infusion relieves rest pain and helps ischaemic ulcers
Used in severe claudication and Raynaud's disease
Intracavernosal alprostadil causes erection for 1 to 2 hours
Oral sildenafil or tadalafil is now preferred

cards.front: Short note: Leukotrienes

points: 5-lipoxygenase with FLAP converts arachidonic acid to LTA4, then to LTB4 and cysteinyl LTs
Made mainly by neutrophils (LTB4) and macrophages (LTC4, LTD4)
LTB4 is a potent chemotactic agent for neutrophils, monocytes and T cells
LTC4 and LTD4 increase capillary permeability and constrict smooth muscle
Cysteinyl LTs increase airway mucus and bronchoconstriction
BLT1 and BLT2 for LTB4
cysLT1 for LTD4 and cysLT2 for LTC4 and LTD4 equally
All signal through Gq and IP3/DAG
Cysteinyl LTs are the most important mediators of human allergic asthma
Montelukast and zafirlukast antagonise cysLT1

cards.front: Short note: Platelet activating factor

points: Acetylglyceryl ether phosphorylcholine
Made on demand by leukocytes, platelets, endothelium and kidney cells
No stored form; active at subnanomolar concentrations
Platelet aggregation and release of TXA2
Neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion and superoxide production
Most potent known agent for increasing vascular permeability
Bronchial asthma with prolonged airway hyper-reactivity
Anaphylactic shock and inflammation
Possible roles in thrombosis and gastric ulceration
Ginkgolide B (plant-derived) and some PAF analogues have been studied, with potential in stroke, claudication, sepsis and MI
Rupatadine, an H1 antihistamine with added PAF antagonism, is used in allergic rhinitis

cards.front: Essay: Prostaglandins, thromboxanes and prostacyclin

points: Eicosanoids are derived from 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acids
Prostaglandins are made by nearly all cells and act locally
Arachidonic acid released by phospholipase A2
Cyclooxygenase gives PGG2 and PGH2, then PGE2, PGF2alpha, PGD2, PGI2 and TXA2 by tissue-specific enzymes
NSAIDs and glucocorticoids inhibit synthesis
PGE2 and PGI2 vasodilate; TXA2 constricts
PGI2 and TXA2 act as opposing controls on platelet aggregation
Uterine contraction and cervical softening
Bronchial constriction (PGF2alpha, PGD2) or dilatation (PGE2)
GI effects: diarrhoea, gastric protection and mucus secretion
Natriuresis, renin release and renal vasodilatation through PGE2 and PGI2
Sensitise nociceptors and cause fever via hypothalamic PGE2
Obstetrics, glaucoma, peptic ulcer, neonatal ductus and pulmonary hypertension
Limited by short action, side effects and cost

cards.front: Essay: Eicosanoids in inflammation and asthma

points: Eicosanoids are local mediators of inflammation
Cyclooxygenase products and lipoxygenase products act together
PGE2 and PGI2 produce vasodilatation, oedema and pain sensitisation
COX-2 is induced at inflamed sites and inhibited by NSAIDs
LTB4 recruits leukocytes; cysteinyl LTs increase permeability
LTs play a greater role in chronic inflammatory states
Imbalance between constrictor PGs, TXA2 and cysteinyl LTs and dilator PGE2
Aspirin-sensitive asthma may come from diversion of arachidonic acid to LTC4 and LTD4
Antihistamines have little effect because LTs and PAF dominate
Causes bronchoconstriction and prolonged hyper-reactivity
Recruits eosinophils and promotes oedema
Cysteinyl LT antagonists in asthma
Corticosteroids reduce arachidonic acid release by increasing annexins
NSAIDs can worsen asthma in susceptible patients

cards.front: Classify: prostanoid receptors by signalling
cards.text: The contractile group (EP1, {{FP}}, {{TP}}) couples through {{Gq}}; the relaxant group (DP1, EP2, EP4, {{IP}}) couples through {{Gs}}; {{EP3}} is the inhibitory receptor coupling through Gi.

cards.front: Classify: prostaglandin analogues by use
cards.text: Latanoprost for {{glaucoma}}; misoprostol for {{peptic ulcer}}; alprostadil to keep the {{ductus arteriosus}} patent; epoprostenol for {{pulmonary hypertension}}; carboprost for {{postpartum haemorrhage}}.

cards.front: Classify: leukotriene receptors
cards.text: BLT1 and BLT2 bind {{LTB4}}; cysLT1 binds {{LTD4}} mainly in bronchial and intestinal muscle; cysLT2 is found mainly in {{leukocytes}} and spleen; all signal through {{Gq}}.

cards.front: Classify: eicosanoid sources
cards.text: Platelets synthesise {{TXA2}}; endothelium synthesises {{PGI2}}; macrophages make {{LTC4 and LTD4}}; neutrophils make {{LTB4}}.

cards.front: Short note: Drugs for erectile dysfunction

points: Nitric oxide from nerves and endothelium relaxes corpus cavernosum through cGMP
PDE-5 breaks down cGMP; blocking it potentiates NO
Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil
Sildenafil is taken before intercourse; usual 50 mg, 25 mg if over 65 years
Works only with sexual stimulation
Tadalafil is longer acting, with half-life about 18 h
Androgens only when androgen deficiency is proven
Headache, flushing, nasal congestion, dizziness, fall in BP and dyspepsia
PDE-6 inhibition can impair colour vision
Contraindicated with nitrates: sharp fall in BP, with deaths reported
Priapism risk in leukaemia, sickle cell anaemia and myeloma

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacotherapy of peptic ulcer disease

points: Omeprazole is the prototype; it irreversibly inactivates the H+/K+ ATPase
Preferred over H2 blockers for peptic ulcer; faster healing at 40 mg than 20 mg
Inhibit CYP2C19, reducing clopidogrel activation and raising levels of some drugs (e.g. warfarin, phenytoin)
Cimetidine is the prototype; ranitidine is about 5 times as potent
Famotidine is longer acting; about 70% excreted unchanged in urine
Less effective than PPIs for NSAID-induced and H. pylori ulcers
Antacids reduce their absorption; leave a 2-hour gap
Misoprostol is a PGE1 analogue that reduces acid output and protects against NSAID injury
Seldom used now because PPIs are more effective and better tolerated
Neutralise acid rather than reducing production
Acid rebound and increased gastric motility can follow
